'''Jean Marie Carlson''' (born 1962) is a professor of [[complexity]] at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]]. She studies robustness and feedback in highly connected [[complex system]]s, which have applications in a variety of areas including earthquakes, wildfires and neuroscience.

== Early life and education ==
Carlson studied [[electrical engineering]] and [[computer science]] at [[Princeton University]], graduating in 1984. She then moved to [[Cornell University]] for her graduate studies, earning a master's in [[applied physics]]. In 1987, she switched to [[theoretical condensed matter physics]] for her doctoral studies, completing her PhD in 1988. She worked under the supervision of [[James Sethna]] on the [[spin glass]] model in the [[Bethe lattice|Bethe Lattice]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Carlson|first=Jean Marie|date=1988|title=Critical Properties of the Bethe Lattice Spin Glass.|journal=Ph.D. Thesis|bibcode=1988PhDT.......102C}}</ref> Carlson worked in the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics]] as a postdoctoral scholar with [[James S. Langer]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11604024.html|title=Langer, James S.|website=history.aip.org|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sethna.lassp.cornell.edu/people/former-members|title=Former Members {{!}} James Sethna|website=sethna.lassp.cornell.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Carlson was appointed to the faculty at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] in 1990. She works on the fundamental theory and applications of [[complex system]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.icb.ucsb.edu/people/jean-m-carlson|title=Jean M Carlson {{!}} www.icb.ucsb.edu|website=www.icb.ucsb.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14|archive-date=2019-04-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190414151417/https://www.icb.ucsb.edu/people/jean-m-carlson|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://brainucsb.herokuapp.com/people/dr-jean-carlson|title=BRI: UCSB|website=brainucsb.herokuapp.com|access-date=2019-04-14|archive-date=2019-10-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191028025546/http://brainucsb.herokuapp.com/people/dr-jean-carlson|url-status=dead}}</ref> She was awarded a [[David and Lucile Packard Foundation]] fellowship in 1993, which allowed her to study the physical and mathematical principles that underlie complexity.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.packard.org/what-we-fund/science/packard-fellowships-for-science-and-engineering/fellowship-directory/carlson-jean-m/|title=Carlson, Jean M.|website=The David and Lucile Packard Foundation|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-13}}</ref> Carlson uses [[highly optimized tolerance]] (HOT) methods that connect evolving structure with power laws in highly interconnected systems.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/HOToverview.html|title=Highly Optimized Tolerance|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Carlson|first=null|last2=Doyle|first2=null|date=2000-03-13|title=Highly optimized tolerance: robustness and design in complex systems|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=84|issue=11|pages=2529–2532|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.84.2529|issn=1079-7114|pmid=11018927|bibcode=2000PhRvL..84.2529C|url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/1523/1/CARprl00.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/networks.html|title=Networks|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> Carlson developed the HOT mechanism in the early 2000s, and has since applied it to complex systems including the immune system, earthquakes, wildfires and neuroscience. HOT represents a unifying framework that can couple with external environments, which differs from [[self-organized criticality]] and the [[edge of chaos]].<ref name=":0" />

Carlson has used computational systems biology to understand the [[immune system]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/Theoretical%20Immunology/index.html|title=Untitled Document|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-13}}</ref> She studies how the immune system changes with age, as well as [[autoimmune disease]] and [[homeostasis]].<ref name=":1" /> Carlson worked with Eric Jones to develop a mathematical model that can analyse and predict interactions in the [[gut bacteria]] of [[Drosophila melanogaster|fruit flies]]. It is hoped that this model will be able to explain the human [[gut microbiome]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://neurosciencenews.com/microbiome-model-10306/|title=Modeling the Microbiome|date=2018-12-05|website=Neuroscience News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> Their model demonstrated that the interaction between bacteria in the gut are as important to the overall health of a fruit fly as their presence in the gut.<ref name=":2" />

Carlson has also applied complexity theory to [[neuroscience]], identifying the properties of neural [[Neural network|networks]] that are protected in the healthy population.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/neuro.html|title=Neuroscience|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> Understanding these networks could explain the connection between the structure of white matter and cognitive function.<ref name=":3" /> Carlson looks to explain how neural networks are involved with learning and memory, by comparing them to computational and biological  information processing structures.<ref name=":3" /> Carlson is particularly interested in sequential learning; which combines new information with previous knowledge.<ref name=":3" /> Her work combines computational models with experimental data from [[electroencephalography]] and [[magnetic resonance imaging]].<ref name=":3" /> She demonstrated that the parts of the brain that synchronise their activity during memory-related tasks become smaller but more numerous as people age.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://neurosciencenews.com/age-memory-activity-5591/|title=Missed Connections: Memory Related Brain Activity Loses Cohesion As We Age|date=2016-11-23|website=Neuroscience News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>

The application of [[statistical mechanics]] to [[materials science]] could help to describe the characteristics of [[granular material]]s.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/granular.html|title=Granular Materials|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> She applies [[Shear transformation|shear transformation zone]] theory to [[granular material]] to describe how they flow and jam.<ref name=":4" /> This work contributes to her studies of friction in [[earthquake fault]]s, rate-and-state laws and rheological chaos.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/constitutive.html|title=Constitutive Laws|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=0606092|title=NSF Award Search: Award#0606092 - Friction, Fatigue and Failure: a Multiscale Approach Linking Physics, Fabrication and Geophysical Phenomena|website=www.nsf.gov|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> Carlson has studied complexity in several areas of earthquake physics, including dynamic rupture and supershear.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/earthquakes.html|title=Earthquakes|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref>  She developed an algorithm (Highly Optimized Tolerance Fire Spread Model, HFire) that can model the spread of a wildfire, which can be used to understand the longterm evolution of forest ecosystems and helping to coordinate forest management. She has investigated human decision-making in disaster response, in an effort to make evacuations more safe and effective.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/disasters.html|title=Disaster|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-13}}</ref> She has investigated the tradeoffs that arise in [[wildfire]] response, using models of the economy, populations and fire spread.<ref name=":5" /> This requires dynamic decision tools, as time delays can result in more fires and demand for resources.<ref name=":5" /> She has also studied how information networks impact decisions, and the relationship between information dissemination and social sharing.<ref name=":5" />

Carlson has also applied complexity theory to [[econophysics]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/econophysics.html|title=Econophysics|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> evolution<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/evolution.html|title=Ecology and Forest Fires|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> and [[control theory]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://web.physics.ucsb.edu/~complex/research/controls.html|title=Control theory|website=web.physics.ucsb.edu|access-date=2019-04-14}}</ref> She holds visiting professorships at [[Santa Fe Institute]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.santafe.edu//people/profile/jean-carlson|title=Jean Carlson {{!}} Santa Fe Institute|website=www.santafe.edu|language=en|access-date=2019-04-14|archive-date=2019-05-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190514192652/https://santafe.edu/people/profile/jean-carlson|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Recognition==
Carlson was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (APS) in 2021, after a nomination from the APS Topical Group on Statistical and Nonlinear Physics, "for the development of mathematically rigorous, physics-based models of nonlinear and complex systems that have significantly impacted a broad range of fields including neuroscience, environmental science, and geophysics".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2021&unit_id=GSNP&institution=|title=Fellows nominated in 2021 by the Topical Group on Statistical and Nonlinear Physics|work=APS Fellows archive|publisher=American Physical Society|access-date=2021-10-22}}</ref>
